  Over the course of 10 weeks, I worked in a team of 4 to ideate, prototype, design, and assemble a solution for our project users, who are nonambulatory residents at the Misericordia Home living with limited upper limb mobility, like hemiplegia. Since there is a wide range of reduced motor coordination among users, we needed a solution that would reduce physical exertion and fatigue for users with very impaired accessibilty. In particular, we opted to create an electronic solution that would best help two users who retained the use of just two fingers, and had difficulty moving the rest of their upper arms, as seen below (reproduced with project partner permission and faces cropped for privacy).

Device Functionality Overview

  The PLUM is a hand-held device with four directional keys and two mouse-click buttons that allow the user to navigate a computer screen. Access to a keyboard is managed through an on-screen keyboard, allowing the user to type without reaching for an external peripheral, which can be extremely physically and mentally taxing. The device itself can be worn on either the left or right hand, with an accessible Velcro strap that can be easily adjusted without outside assistance.   Internally, the PLUM's buttons go through an RJ-45 (ethernet) cable to a "Makey-Makey" microcontroller housed in a small black box, which is itself plugged in to the user's desktop computer. Personal Contributions

  I'm proud to have worked on more of the technical side of the project. Specifically, I created the necessary parts in Fusion360, using Bambu printers to rapid-prototype parts. Additionally, I soldered the internal ethernet adapter (which had to be sanded down to fit into the tight form factor) to the buttons. We tested the buttons with our users to make sure that we picked the most accessible ones, and we enlarged the left/right-click buttons so they'd be most accessible. In charge of materials procurement, as well as logging purchases on the debit card / budget we were given. Heard of the makey-makey device from our project partner. Even though it appeared to be a simple kid's toy, I found it particularly useful in mapping a user's inputs to keyboard controls without specialty software. Since it was made to be safe for kids, it meant that I could save space in the handheld portion of the PLUM without worrying about adding a pull-down network (reword this maybe?) At the end of the project, we also tabled at the end-of-quarter exposition, explaining our design with a live demo. This demo included allowing users to navigate the Northwestern Norris website, perform a short typing test, and attempt to solve the Wordle, all with only the use of the PLUM.
